scenario.title: Observation-level bootstrap manufactures precision
scenario.trap: Resampling observations treats 1,200 nested rows as 1,200 experiments and returns an interval several times too narrow.
scenario.truth: The design supplies 20 independent units. The true mean loss difference is +0.6.
scenario.defence: Resample whole units; observations travel with the unit they belong to.
scenario.can_conclude: That the observation-level interval under-covers by a margin larger than Monte Carlo error at this number of replications.
scenario.cannot_conclude: That the unit-level interval is calibrated at 20 units -- measured coverage there is below nominal too, just far less so.

naive.analysis: iid bootstrap over observations, both arms independent

findings.finding: observation-level resampling understates uncertainty
findings.detail: The unit-level interval is 3.9x wider. The naive analysis claims 1200 independent units where the design supplies 20.

findings.finding: the understatement shows up as measurable under-coverage
findings.detail: observation-level (pseudoreplicated) bootstrap: 55.0% coverage of a nominal 95% interval (R=200, MC SE 0.035, 95% Wilson CI [48.1%, 61.7%]) versus world_id-level cluster bootstrap: 91.5% coverage of a nominal 95% interval (R=200, MC SE 0.020, 95% Wilson CI [86.8%, 94.6%]). The two coverage estimates differ by 0.36 (MC SE 0.040), so the gap is not Monte Carlo noise.

scenario.title: Unit-level bootstrap coverage, with its Monte Carlo error
scenario.trap: One interval establishes nothing on its own, and a bare coverage percentage from 100 replications is read as if it were exact.
scenario.truth: The true mean loss difference is +0.6 in every replication.
scenario.defence: Report empirical coverage with its Monte Carlo SE and a Wilson interval, and compare coverage at two unit counts.
scenario.can_conclude: That coverage improves with more units and is consistent with nominal at 60 units.
scenario.cannot_conclude: That the percentile interval is calibrated at 20 units; the Wilson interval there excludes the nominal level.

findings.finding: unit-level coverage approaches nominal as units are added
findings.detail: At 20 units: world_id-level cluster bootstrap: 91.5% coverage of a nominal 95% interval (R=200, MC SE 0.020, 95% Wilson CI [86.8%, 94.6%]) -- the Monte Carlo interval excludes the nominal level, so this is real under-coverage, not noise. At 60 units: world_id-level cluster bootstrap: 95.0% coverage of a nominal 95% interval (R=200, MC SE 0.015, 95% Wilson CI [91.0%, 97.3%]).

findings.finding: more observations per unit cannot repair an observation-level interval
findings.detail: The observation-level interval narrows as observations are added while its coverage stays broken, because the missing variance is between units. Only more units buy precision that generalises.

scenario.title: Mean favours A while the harmful tail favours B
scenario.trap: policy_a has the lower average loss, so a mean-only report recommends it.
scenario.truth: policy_a carries a 4% per-observation chance of a +60 loss; its 90% CVaR is far worse than policy_b's while its mean is 0.8 better.
scenario.defence: Declare tail metrics in advance, orient them by the metric's direction, and report the disagreement with both intervals.
scenario.can_conclude: That the two contrasts point in opposite directions, each with its own interval.
scenario.cannot_conclude: Which policy is preferable; that needs a risk preference declared outside the analysis.

truth.design: policy_a shifts loss down by 3.2 but carries a 4% chance of a +60 spike per observation, worth +2.4 on average -- a net mean advantage of 0.8 bought with a heavy upper tail

naive.conclusion_if_reported_alone: mean_loss: the 95% interval for the estimated difference (policy_b - policy_a) is (0.3655, 1.332) and excludes 0, favouring policy_a on this metric, paired on 60 shared world_id.

correct.analysis: report central and tail contrasts together, with both intervals

scenario.title: Equivalent within a declared margin
scenario.trap: The interval includes zero, so the report is read as a finding that the policies match.
scenario.truth: The true difference is +0.03 against a declared margin of +/-0.40 -- real, and negligible at that margin.
scenario.defence: TOST against the declared margin, with the decision caveat attached.
scenario.can_conclude: That the contrast lies inside the predeclared margin.
scenario.cannot_conclude: That the policies are interchangeable in use; the margin's adequacy is a domain judgement.

truth.design: a real but negligible difference, with enough units to resolve it

naive.analysis: read a zero-containing interval as a finding of equivalence
naive.why_wrong: An interval that includes zero is consistent with zero and with every other value it contains. Without a margin it cannot distinguish a negligible difference from an unresolved one.

correct.analysis: TOST against a declared margin, with the decision caveat attached

margin.source: declared in the scenario definition before any data was generated

correct.interpretation: Equivalent within the declared margin +/-0.4: the 90% interval for the estimated difference (-0.09097, 0.08149) lies inside it.
caveats: STATISTICALLY_EQUIVALENT is not OPERATIONALLY_INTERCHANGEABLE: this is a statement that the estimated contrast lies inside the predeclared margin, not that the alternatives are interchangeable in use. Whether the margin marks a decision-relevant difference is a domain judgement outside this library.

findings.finding: equivalence needs a margin, and with one it is concludable
findings.detail: Equivalent within the declared margin +/-0.4: the 90% interval for the estimated difference (-0.09097, 0.08149) lies inside it.

findings.finding: statistical equivalence is not operational interchangeability
findings.detail: The verdict states that the contrast lies inside a predeclared margin. Whether that margin marks a decision-relevant difference is a domain judgement the library does not make.

scenario.title: Units that share a higher-level shock
scenario.trap: 80 units look like 80 replicates, so a unit-level cluster bootstrap looks correct and is not.
scenario.truth: The units come in 20 groups of 4 sharing an event-level shock that acts differently on the two policies, so there are 20 independent replicates.
scenario.defence: Declare the inference structure and check it against the records; an event that contains units is refused as a nested level.
scenario.can_conclude: That resampling at the wrong level under-covers even though it is a cluster bootstrap.
scenario.cannot_conclude: That the library can detect an unrecorded dependence; it can only see groupings that appear in the records.

truth.design: 80 units, but each group of 4 shares one event. The event carries a shock that affects the two policies DIFFERENTLY, so it does not cancel in the paired difference. The event is a level ABOVE the unit: there are 20 independent replicates, not 80.

naive.analysis: declare world_id as the independent unit
naive.refused_with:
the declared inference structure contradicts the records:
  [inverted_nesting] the records say 'world_id' is nested inside 'event_id', but the configuration declares 'event_id' as nested inside 'world_id'. The independent unit is 'event_id', not 'world_id'. Declare inference.primary_unit: event_id -- resampling 'world_id' would break up a dependent group and understate uncertainty, which is the same error as resampling observations.

correct.analysis: declare event_id as the independent unit (events contain units here)

findings.finding: a unit-level bootstrap fails when units share a higher-level shock
findings.detail: Resampling the 80 units gives world_id-level cluster bootstrap: 78.7% coverage of a nominal 95% interval (R=150, MC SE 0.033, 95% Wilson CI [71.4%, 84.5%]); resampling the 20 shared events gives event_id-level cluster bootstrap: 93.3% coverage of a nominal 95% interval (R=150, MC SE 0.020, 95% Wilson CI [88.2%, 96.3%]). Cluster resampling is only correct at the level where independence actually holds, and 'cluster bootstrap' is not a synonym for 'correct'.

scenario.title: Runs that crash on the hardest units
scenario.trap: policy_b's crashed runs are treated as missing values and dropped, so it is scored only where it survived.
scenario.truth: policy_b is worse by +1.0, and its runs crash on the 18 hardest units.
scenario.defence: Keep failed runs in the records with a status, declare the mechanism, and report a worst-case bound beside the complete-case estimate.
scenario.can_conclude: The complete-case contrast and a bound on how far the missing runs could move it.
scenario.cannot_conclude: The target-population contrast; no method recovers outcomes that were never produced.

truth.design: policy_b's runs crash on the 18 hardest units. The rows are still present with a `crashed` status and null outcomes, so the failure is visible rather than absent.

naive.analysis: drop the crashed runs and analyse what is left
naive.why_wrong: The runs that crashed are the hard ones. Complete-case analysis then describes the units where policy_b happened to survive.

correct.analysis: keep the failures visible, declare the mechanism, and bound the estimate

scenario.title: Many observations, almost no replicates
scenario.trap: A 90% CVaR computed from 5 units is reported like any other number.
scenario.truth: Every design here has 160 observations per unit; only the unit count varies, from 5 to 50.
scenario.defence: Per-estimator credibility thresholds, so the warning matches the statistic instead of a universal minimum n.
scenario.can_conclude: Which statistics the available unit count can support.
scenario.cannot_conclude: A universal minimum sample size; the threshold depends on the estimator.

correct.analysis: per-metric credibility thresholds, so the warning matches the statistic

findings.finding: credibility is metric-specific, not a universal minimum n
findings.detail: `mean` is flagged below 5 units, `cvar` and `quantile` below 20, `max`/`min` below 30. A single global threshold would either pass a meaningless CVaR or block a usable mean.

findings.finding: interval width shrinks with units, not with observations
findings.detail: Every design here has 160 observations per unit. Only the unit count changes, and only the unit count narrows the intervals.

scenario.title: CVaR summarising the beneficial tail
scenario.trap: A higher-is-better metric analysed with an upper-tail CVaR describes the best events and calls the result risk.
scenario.truth: policy_a has the higher mean success rate and a much heavier low tail.
scenario.defence: `tail: harmful` resolves against the declared direction; a contradictory `params.tail` is rejected at config load.
scenario.can_conclude: The contrast in the harmful tail, with the tail side printed beside it.
scenario.cannot_conclude: Anything about the harmful tail from a beneficial-tail statistic, however confident its interval looks.

truth.design: policy_a has the higher mean success rate but a heavy LOW tail: one event in ten is a whole-event disaster in which success collapses.

naive.analysis: CVaR with the upper tail on a higher-is-better metric
naive.why_wrong: For a higher-is-better metric the harmful end is the LOW end. Averaging the best 10% of events describes the good case and calls it risk.

correct.analysis: `tail: harmful` resolved against the declared orientation
correct.definition: CVaR at alpha=0.9 in the lower tail of event_id-level values of `mission_success`: the unweighted mean of the k = max(1, ceil((1-alpha)*n)) most extreme values, with (1-alpha)*n rounded to 9 decimals before the ceiling, and ties included by position in the sorted order

findings.finding: tail side follows orientation, so it cannot be chosen by accident
findings.detail: `tail: harmful` with `direction: higher_is_better` resolves to the lower tail. Writing `params: {tail: upper}` alongside `tail: harmful` is rejected by the config loader as a contradiction; overriding requires saying `tail: upper` explicitly, which is then visible in the report and the provenance.

scenario.title: A symmetric margin that hides an unacceptable loss
scenario.trap: A symmetric +/-0.50 margin declares a 0.25 increase in loss negligible.
scenario.truth: policy_b is 0.25 worse, and only 0.15 of extra loss was acceptable.
scenario.defence: Support asymmetric margins, and record each margin's source.
scenario.can_conclude: Whether the contrast lies inside the margin that was actually declared.
scenario.cannot_conclude: Which margin is correct; the library checks arithmetic against a declaration, not the declaration itself.

truth.design: policy_b is 0.25 worse. A symmetric +/-0.50 margin calls that negligible; an asymmetric margin that tolerates only 0.15 of extra loss does not.

naive.analysis: a symmetric margin because symmetry is the default in most software

correct.analysis: the margin the decision actually implies, asymmetric and documented

margin.source: asymmetric tolerance: extra loss is less acceptable than less loss

caveats: The margin is asymmetric: 0.5 tolerated below zero, 0.15 above. The equivalence region is not centred on zero.

findings.finding: the equivalence verdict depends on the margin, as it must

scenario.title: An interval that runs past the end of the scale
scenario.trap: A basic bootstrap interval on a rate near 1.0 includes values above 1.0 and is reported without comment.
scenario.truth: The metric is a proportion with declared support [0, 1].
scenario.defence: Declare the support, check the endpoints, report the violation, and do not clamp.
scenario.can_conclude: That the interval construction does not suit this metric here.
scenario.cannot_conclude: A corrected interval; the library flags the problem rather than silently substituting a different method.

truth.design: a success rate pushed close to its upper bound of 1.0, with only 8 units. The sampling distribution is squeezed against the boundary and is left-skewed, so reflecting it about the estimate sends the upper endpoint past 1.

naive.analysis: a basic (reflected) bootstrap interval on a rate near its bound

bounds_check.note: Interval endpoints lie outside the metric's declared support. They are reported unclamped: truncating them would understate the interval's width without making the construction appropriate. Consider an interval on a transformed scale.

naive.why_wrong: The basic interval reflects the bootstrap distribution about the estimate. Near a boundary the reflection lands outside the support, so the interval includes values the metric cannot take.

correct.analysis: declare the support, report the violation, do not clamp

findings.finding: an impossible endpoint is reported, never silently clamped
findings.detail: Truncating the endpoint at 1.0 would narrow the interval without making the construction appropriate, and would hide that the method does not suit a bounded outcome. The library reports the violation and leaves the number alone.

findings.finding: the interval construction is part of the result
findings.detail: Percentile endpoints are order statistics of the resampled estimates, so they stay inside the observed support; basic endpoints need not. The two are not interchangeable, and which one was used belongs in the report.

scenario.title: Twenty null metrics, uncorrected
scenario.trap: Twenty exploratory contrasts on pure noise are reported individually and some of them resolve.
scenario.truth: Every one of the twenty columns has a true difference of exactly zero.
scenario.defence: Assign each metric a role, declare the family, and apply Holm across it.
scenario.can_conclude: Which findings survive correction over the family that was declared.
scenario.cannot_conclude: Anything about a family the configuration did not declare; the library will not infer one.

truth.design: 20 outcome columns generated with no policy effect at all, analysed as one declared exploratory family alongside a null primary metric.

naive.analysis: run 21 comparisons and report whichever resolve

correct.analysis: declare the family by analysis role and apply Holm to it

findings.finding: an uncorrected family of 20 null tests resolves some of them
findings.detail: Every noise column has a true difference of exactly 0. 1 contrast(s) still resolved at the 95% level, which is what a family of 20 independent tests is expected to do.

findings.finding: correction requires a declared family, and the library will not guess one
findings.detail: The family here is the declared `secondary` role. Holm is applied across it and the primary metric is left uncorrected. The confidence intervals shown are marginal: adjusted p-values and unadjusted intervals appear side by side, labelled as such.

scenario.title: A crashed run counted as a missing value
scenario.trap: policy_b crashes on 22% of runs; dropping those runs makes it look better.
scenario.truth: policy_b raises the success rate of the runs that finish while failing to finish more than a fifth of them.
scenario.defence: Declare how each run status is handled; counting a crash as a failure keeps it in the denominator.
scenario.can_conclude: That the finding's sign depends on the declared handling, and what each handling gives.
scenario.cannot_conclude: Which handling is right; that is a domain question the library forces into the open rather than answering.

truth.design: policy_b raises the success rate of the runs that complete, but 22% of its runs crash and produce nothing. Whether that is an improvement depends entirely on how a crash is counted.

naive.analysis: treat a crashed run as a missing value and drop it
naive.why_wrong: The crashed runs leave the denominator, so a policy that fails to produce a result is scored only on the occasions when it did.

correct.analysis: count a failed run as a failed observation, as declared
correct.note: Which handling is right is a domain question. The library's job is to make the choice explicit, record it, and show that the two answers differ.

findings.finding: the sign of the finding depends on how a failed run is counted
findings.detail: Dropping crashes gives +0.0640 favouring policy_b; counting them as failures gives -0.1589 favouring policy_a. Same records, opposite conclusions, and the difference is a declaration rather than a computation.

findings.finding: failed runs never leave the accounting
findings.detail: The run-status ledger counts every run by policy and status before any row is handled, so the reader can see the crash rate even under the handling that drops them.

lines: policy_b raises the success rate of the runs that complete, but 22% of its runs crash and produce nothing. Whether that is an improvement depends entirely on how a crash is counted.
WRONG  crashes -> missing, then dropped: +0.0640 [+0.0489, +0.0793] -> favours policy_b
RIGHT  crashes -> counted as failures:   -0.1589 [-0.2129, -0.1057] -> favours policy_a
run status ledger:
policy_a   completed      completed            rows=3600
policy_b   completed      completed            rows=2680
policy_b   crashed        failure              rows=920

scenario.title: Paired data analysed as two independent arms
scenario.trap: A fully paired design compared arm-to-arm loses a real effect in unit variance.
scenario.truth: Every unit carries both policies; the unit SD is 4.0 and the effect is 0.9.
scenario.defence: Pair within unit by default, and label any unpaired comparison as such everywhere it appears.
scenario.can_conclude: That discarding the pairing widens the interval enough to change the finding.
scenario.cannot_conclude: That pairing is always available; when units are not shared, the estimand changes rather than the precision.

truth.design: a fully paired design: every unit carries both policies, and the unit effect (SD 4.0) is far larger than the policy effect (0.9).

naive.analysis: ignore the pairing and compare two arms
notes: UNPAIRED RESAMPLE (comparison.paired: false): each arm was resampled independently, so unit-level variation does not cancel in the difference. On data where units are shared this discards the design's precision.

correct.analysis: pair within unit, so the unit effect cancels

findings.finding: discarding the pairing discards the design's precision
findings.detail: The unpaired interval is 7.4x wider and no longer resolves a real effect. Nothing about the data changed; the analysis threw away the structure that made the comparison sharp.

findings.finding: an unpaired analysis of paired data is labelled, not silently accepted
findings.detail: Every result from `require_common_units: false` carries an UNPAIRED note through the panel, the interval, the console output and the report.

lines: a fully paired design: every unit carries both policies, and the unit effect (SD 4.0) is far larger than the policy effect (0.9).
true difference: +0.900
WRONG  unpaired: +0.966 [-1.237, +3.146]  width 4.383  -> inconclusive
RIGHT  paired:   +0.966 [+0.672, +1.265]  width 0.593  -> worse
width ratio: 7.4x

scenario.title: Choosing the headline metric after seeing the results
scenario.trap: Twelve exploratory metrics carry no effect, one of them looks favourable, and it becomes the headline.
scenario.truth: policy_b is genuinely worse on the declared primary metric by +0.55.
scenario.defence: Exactly one primary metric, reported first; every other finding labelled with its role and corrected within its declared family.
scenario.can_conclude: The primary contrast, and that the favourable exploratory ones are consistent with noise.
scenario.cannot_conclude: That the analysis was preregistered; `analysis_status` records the claim and the existence of a config file is not evidence for it.

truth.design: policy_b is genuinely worse on the declared primary metric. Forty exploratory columns carry no effect at all, and some of them will look favourable.

naive.analysis: report the most favourable metric as the headline

correct.analysis: declared roles, primary reported first, exploratory labelled and corrected

findings.finding: with enough exploratory metrics, one of them always looks good
findings.detail: 13 of 40 pure-noise metrics point towards policy_b, and the most convincing of them has raw p = 0.052. Choosing the headline after seeing them is the error; no correction applied afterwards repairs it.

findings.finding: role discipline is structural, not advisory
findings.detail: Exactly one metric may be declared primary; the loader rejects a second. The report prints the primary outcome first, labels every other finding with its role, and records `analysis_status` so a reader can see whether any of this was declared in advance at all.

PRIMARY (declared)  mean_loss: +0.421 [+0.083, +0.773] -> favours policy_a
SHOPPED (exploratory) noise_03: -0.074 [-0.160, +0.001] -> favours None, raw p=0.052, adjusted p=1.0
13 of 40 noise metrics point at policy_b; 0 of them resolve at the 95% level
